clue.text: One prepared to put two and two together ?

definitions.text: One prepared to put two and two together ?

parts.words: One prepared to put two and two together
parts.note: read as someone always ready to add up figures, or a booklet of pre-worked sums kept to hand for doing arithmetic

explanation.surface: A sharp detective, always ready to connect the clues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put two and two together' suggests deduction, but here it is plain addition: the answer is a book of ready-made calculations, and also, word for word, a prepared calculator.
explanation.definitionFit: A book of tables giving the results of common calculations is ready (prepared) and does the reckoning (adding up) for you.

clue.text: Organize challenge — a punishing experience

parts.note: to organize a business or event is to run it
throwing down the gauntlet issues a challenge, so the gauntlet stands for the challenge itself

explanation.surface: Someone sets up a contest that turns out to be an ordeal.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses of 'gauntlet' meet: the glove thrown down as a challenge, and the double line of men who beat a victim forced to pass between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To run the gauntlet was originally to be beaten while passing between two rows of attackers, so it names any punishing ordeal.

clue.text: Snake on the cold lunch counter ?

definitions.meaning: an old poetic word for the asp, the small venomous serpent
a savoury jelly in which cold meats or eggs are set, served at a cold buffet

explanation.surface: A serpent slithers along the counter where the cold buffet is laid out.
explanation.walkthrough: The obvious move is ASP plus something; but the whole word is itself an archaic name for the snake, and also the jelly of a cold buffet.
explanation.definitionFit: Poets once used the word for the venomous asp, and the same word names the meat jelly that sits on a cold-food counter.

clue.text: By. whom you are unaided

parts.note: read 'by whom' as asking who did it when you did it with no help: the people doing it were you, by your own unaided efforts

explanation.walkthrough: The stray full stop after 'By' is OCR noise. Doing something 'by' this plural pronoun means doing it alone, so it answers 'by whom' for an unaided group.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something on your own, with no help, is doing it by your own persons, the plural reflexive pronoun.

clue.text: Part of the serial is in a form of poem

indicators.note: 'is in' places the little word inside the poem form, so the poem is cut open to hold it

parts.note: an epode is a lyric form, a couplet of long and short lines, or the third part of an ode

explanation.surface: A literary critic notes that one instalment of a serial is written in verse.
explanation.walkthrough: An epode is a classical lyric form, often the closing stanza of a Greek ode; 'in' puts the clue's own 'is' inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A serial is broadcast or printed in instalments, and each instalment is one part of the whole story.

clue.text: What a bloody tie, his pink creation!

indicators.note: a creation is something newly made, so the letters of these two words are made into something new

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at a garish pink necktie someone else has designed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'creation' rearranges HIS PINK. 'Bloody' looks like a British swear word aimed at the tie, but means 'of blood': a blood tie, family relationship.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie of blood is a family relationship, the bond between relatives.

clue.text: Prison's the devil

definitions.meaning: British slang for a jail or police station
A traditional English nickname for Satan

explanation.surface: A convict says being locked up is hell.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang calls a jail 'the nick', and 'Old Nick' has long been a name for Satan.

clue.text: Salesman Leonard has his problem with a refill order

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative
Len is the usual short form of the name Leonard

indicators.note: his problem means the little word his is in a muddle, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A travelling salesman named Leonard struggles to fill a repeat order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'problem' rearranges 'his' into ISH. The definition is read as an order, an instruction to refill, matching the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An order to refill is the command to fill up again, to restock.

clue.text: Her maid Betty was really Charlie, pretending

definitions.text: Her maid Betty was really Charlie, pretending

parts.words: Her maid Betty was really Charlie, pretending
parts.note: after Culloden in 1746 Bonnie Prince Charlie escaped to Skye disguised as an Irish maid called Betty Burke, the servant of a Highland woman

explanation.surface: A lady discovers her housemaid Betty is a man in disguise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' is not a stray man but Bonnie Prince Charlie, the Stuart pretender to the British throne; 'pretending' points both to the disguise and to his being the Young Pretender.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jacobite heroine of Skye smuggled the fugitive prince to safety, passing him off as her Irish spinning-maid.

clue.text: Like the god Pan, in tune for a change

indicators.note: a change of the letters is called for, so the three words are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: The god Pan, for once, plays his pipes in tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for a change' rearranges PAN, IN and TUNE. 'The god' is not Pan himself but the Roman god of the sea; Pan is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things relating to the Roman sea god or to the planet named after him.

clue.text: Resin, the fuel with a soft centre

indicators.note: a soft centre means the soft letter is set in the middle of the fuel word

parts.note: coal is the fuel burnt in fires and furnaces
p, piano, is the music marking for soft

explanation.surface: A chocolate-box description: a resinous sweet with a soft filling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with a soft centre' puts P (piano, soft) in the middle of COAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Copal is a hard tree resin from the tropics, used in varnishes.

clue.text: Cheat gets round in such a roundabout way

indicators.note: gets round in means the round letter goes inside the turned word
a roundabout way is going backwards, so the word such is read in reverse

parts.note: O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A swindler wriggles out of things in a devious manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in such a roundabout way' turns SUCH into HCUS, and 'in' puts O, the round letter, inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To hocus is to trick or hoax, as in hocus-pocus, a conjuror's deception.

clue.text: The emperor might have given a hoot

indicators.note: the letters of the word hoot could be given out in another order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: An emperor so unconcerned he might not have given a hoot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might have given' rearranges HOOT. Otho was a Roman emperor who reigned for three months in AD 69, the Year of the Four Emperors.
explanation.definitionFit: Otho was briefly ruler of Rome in AD 69 before taking his own life.

clue.text: Brand of gun-catch

definitions.meaning: to brand is to burn a mark into something with a hot iron
the catch in a gun's lock that holds the hammer at cock until the trigger releases it

explanation.surface: A make of firearm safety catch.
explanation.definitionFit: Searing scorches a mark into skin, as branding does, and the same word names the catch in a gun's firing mechanism.

clue.text: Commit Peter, running wild round the rose-red city

indicators.note: round says the scrambled name goes around the city, holding it inside
running wild means the letters of the name are out of control, rearranged

parts.note: Petra in Jordan is the 'rose-red city half as old as time' of Burgon's poem

explanation.surface: Peter is jailed for running amok around the ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running wild' gives PER...TE from the name, which 'round' wraps around the city. Petra is the rose-red city carved into rock in Jordan.
explanation.definitionFit: To commit a crime is to carry it out, which is what a wrongdoer does with a deed.

clue.text: A girl, one Annabel, by the sea

parts.note: gal is an informal word for a girl
I is the Roman numeral one
Annabel Lee is the heroine of Poe's poem, who lived 'in a kingdom by the sea'

explanation.surface: A girl called Annabel lives by the sea, as in Poe's poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by the sea' recalls Poe's line, but 'the sea' is the definition: the Sea of Galilee in Israel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake in northern Israel, called a sea in the Gospels.

clue.text: Washed under in a Kent harbour rising.

indicators.note: under in the harbour means the word under sits inside the harbour name
in a down clue rising means the harbour name is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: Deal is a port town on the coast of Kent, south-east England

explanation.surface: Something gets a soaking under the water in a harbour on the Kent coast.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'rising' reads the port upwards, LAED, and 'in' puts the clue's 'under' inside it. Deal is a small port on the Kent coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Laundered clothes have been washed, and the word is used for money cleaned of its criminal origin.

clue.text: The first thing a bondman hopes for ?

definitions.text: The first thing a bondman hopes for ?

parts.words: The first thing a bondman hopes for
parts.note: a 'bondman' here is not a slave but a holder of British government savings bonds, whose monthly draw pays out prizes, first prize above all

explanation.surface: A slave dreams of freedom above all else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bondman' suggests a serf, but it is a holder of Premium Bonds, a British savings scheme that pays prizes in a lottery instead of interest.
explanation.definitionFit: A premium is a prize or bonus, the kind of reward a bondholder hopes to win.

clue.text: Instrument which in short would cost an evangelist a pound

definitions.text: Instrument which in short would cost an evangelist a pound

parts.words: Instrument which in short would cost an evangelist a pound
parts.note: the instrument's short name is what is left of the gospel writer Luke's name once the L, for pound, is taken away

explanation.surface: A preacher pays a pound for a small musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' points at the instrument's abbreviation, UKE; taking L (pound, from the Latin libra) from LUKE, the evangelist, leaves it.
explanation.definitionFit: The ukulele is a small four-stringed guitar from Hawaii, commonly shortened to uke.

clue.text: Express issue'? The first may be valuable

definitions.text: Express issue'? The first may be valuable

parts.words: Express issue'? The first may be valuable
parts.note: the Daily Express is a British newspaper: one day's printing of it is one of these, and a book's first one is prized by collectors

explanation.surface: Collectors prize the earliest copies of a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Express' looks like a verb, but it is the Daily Express, a British national newspaper; the stray apostrophe is OCR noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's print run for a day is an issue, and a book's first printing is prized by collectors.

clue.text: Like Byron's burning and singing lover

definitions.text: Like Byron's burning and singing lover

parts.words: Like Byron's burning and singing lover
parts.note: Byron's 'The Isles of Greece' opens 'Where burning Sappho loved and sung', so this means relating to that poet of Lesbos

explanation.surface: A passionate lover from one of Byron's poems.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes Byron's Don Juan: 'The isles of Greece, the isles of Greece! Where burning Sappho loved and sung'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes the Greek lyric poet of Lesbos, her verse form, or love between women.

clue.text: Do pigs come, about .500 pounds?

indicators.note: the pigs come about, that is go around, the number and the money

parts.note: swine is a word for pigs
D is the Roman numeral 500
L, from Latin libra, stands for pounds

explanation.surface: A farmer asks whether the pigs weigh about five hundred pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'come about' wraps SWINE around D (500) and L (pounds). 'Do' is the verb, to cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: To do someone, in informal British usage, is to cheat or con them.

clue.text: This sum's substantial (and no messing )

definitions.meaning: a large amount of money, so the word means sizeable
with no mess, neat and orderly

explanation.surface: A large sum of money, handed over neatly and with no fuss.
explanation.definitionFit: A tidy sum is a considerable one, and a tidy room is neat with nothing out of place.

clue.text: Two soldiers thank heaven for this little girl

definitions.text: thank heaven for this little girl

indicators.note: two signals the soldier word is written twice in succession

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: Two soldiers sing their gratitude for a little girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two' doubles GI, the American soldier. 'Thank Heaven for Little Girls' is the opening song of the musical film of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical's title heroine is the young Parisian girl celebrated in the song 'Thank Heaven for Little Girls'.

clue.text: Time-barred ?.

parts.note: read as musical time, time divided into bars, the speed at which a piece is played

explanation.walkthrough: 'Time-barred' is a legal term for a claim that is out of date, but here it means time in musical bars, the speed of the music. The stray full stop is OCR noise.
explanation.definitionFit: In music the speed of the beat is the time, set out bar by bar in the score.

clue.text: A sort of totem anthem

indicators.note: a sort of here means a sorting, a reordering, of the letters of the pole word

explanation.surface: Worshippers sing a kind of hymn to a carved pole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A sort of' rearranges TOTEM.
explanation.definitionFit: A motet is a short sacred choral piece, the kind of anthem sung in church.

clue.text: But. History shows anything but that!

indicators.note: the two words show, that is display, a run of letters inside them across the break

explanation.surface: A sceptic says the historical record proves the very opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows' displays the run inside 'buT HIStory'. 'That' and 'this' are opposites, so the answer is anything but 'that'. The full stop is OCR noise.
explanation.definitionFit: The demonstrative for something near is the opposite of the one for something far off.

clue.text: Mother makes the beds

definitions.meaning: Mother Nature's other name is Mother ...
soil is what garden beds are made of

explanation.surface: A mother doing the housework, making the beds.
explanation.definitionFit: We speak of 'Mother Earth' as parent of all life, and garden beds are made of soil.

clue.text: The disheartened in one of the USA drink this

indicators.note: the shortened word sits in, inside, the state name

parts.note: Indiana is one of the fifty states of the USA

indicators.note: losing its heart means the middle letter of the word goes

explanation.surface: Someone depressed in an American state finds comfort in a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disheartened' takes the middle letter from 'The', leaving TE, which 'in' places inside the state; 'drink this' is the definition, the tea being drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea grown in India, Assam or Darjeeling, is one of the world's most common drinks.

clue.text: Unlike axe-grinders ?

parts.note: someone with an axe to grind has a private motive, so the opposite of such people is free of self-interest

explanation.walkthrough: 'Axe-grinders' are not knife sharpeners but people with an axe to grind, a selfish purpose to pursue.
explanation.definitionFit: An impartial person has no personal stake in a matter, unlike someone with a private aim.
